FoMo models the direction of each move with one of two directional
models:

- **von Mises** (Clarke, Hunt & Hughes, 2022a): a weight for each of a
  few preferred directions, each a von Mises bump of fixed width.
- **Fourier-124**: a smooth curve made of the first, second and fourth
  harmonics (a {cos, sin} pair each), added to an item's log-weight. The
  default.

Both were fitted to every real dataset with everything else the same (the
default priors and centring, 4 chains of 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling
iterations), then compared with `fomo_compare()`.

*Note*: this page doesn't fit anything. It reads each dataset's
Fourier-124 fit (made by the dataset's own `fit_<dataset>.R`), and the von
Mises fits and the comparison in `fits/` in this folder, which
`fit_fourier_versus_vonmises.R` makes (about 14 hours on a laptop). See
`examples/real_data/README.md`.

Code: `fourier_versus_vonmises.R`.

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::read_chunk("fourier_versus_vonmises.R")
```

```{r load}
```

## The comparison

One row per dataset and model. `deterministic`: how often the model's
most likely item is the one selected (leaving out each trial's first
selection and any forced last one); `nn`: the same for the
nearest-neighbour rule, and `gain_nn` the model's gain over it. `elpd_diff`
is the leave-one-trial-out (loo) difference from the better model, with
its standard error; `pct_high_k` the percentage of trials whose Pareto k
is above 0.7 (where loo is less reliable), and `robust` whether the
difference holds without those trials.

```{r table}
```

Fourier-124 is better on every dataset, by between 5 and 21 standard
errors. The datasets differ a lot in size, so per trial:

```{r fig-elpd}
#| fig-cap: "The loo difference per trial between von Mises and Fourier-124 (below 0: von Mises is worse), with 2 standard errors."
```

The gain in accuracy is small (at most about 1.5 points): which item
each model rates most likely mostly agrees, so the loo difference comes
mainly from how much probability each gives the item that was selected.

```{r fig-accuracy}
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy of each model and of the nearest-neighbour rule, per dataset."
```

Stacking weights split the predictions between the models: the weights
of the mixture of the two models' predictive distributions that best
predicts held-out trials. They are not the probability that each model
is right. Von Mises keeps 9-20% of the weight on every dataset, despite
being thousands of elpd behind on some: a mixture gains from von Mises
if it predicts some trials better than Fourier-124, even when it is worse
overall. Which trials those are hasn't been checked yet, so don't read
much into the weights.

```{r fig-stacking}
#| fig-cap: "Stacking weights of the two models, per dataset."
```

## The directional curves

Why Fourier-124 fits better: the directional preferences each model
finds, as log-weights against the absolute direction of the move.

```{r curves}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr file.mtime(c(map_chr(names(datasets), fourier_file), map_chr(names(datasets), vonmises_file)))
```

```{r fig-curves}
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-cap: "Directional log-weight curves (centred), 53% and 97% HPDIs, for each dataset and condition."
```
